strengths: Novel theoretical identification that Tweedie-based training-free guidance is suboptimal (Proposition 3.2), with clear decomposition into low-density, reward, and KL regularization terms

Creative and well-motivated integration of stochastic optimal control and Stein variational inference for diffusion guidance; back-and-forth correction trick elegantly avoids expensive Jacobian computations
Strong empirical results with dramatic improvements (e.g., 2.933% → 25.744% for 5ht1b), convincing ablation study showing SDG without Stein correction often performs worse than baselines

Comprehensive experimental analysis including sampling dynamics visualization (Figures 5, 9-10), multiple evaluation metrics, extreme low-density experiments (40% validity at α_E=0.7), and molecular docking pose visualization
Clear presentation with effective illustration (Figure 1), explicit algorithm description (Algorithm 1), and thorough experimental details in appendix including hyperparameter specifications
weaknesses: Loose theoretical guarantees: Proposition 3.2 provides upper bound with D_KL(q||p) but offers no analysis of bound tightness; only one SVGD step per timestep applied without convergence analysis; approximation error from back-and-forth correction not quantified; no formal proof connecting KL divergence minimization to improved guidance performance

Severely limited experimental scope with validation on only one domain (molecular generation); while Section 3.4 extends to graphs, this is not experimentally validated beyond molecular graphs; claims of broad applicability unsupported
No quantification of computational overhead; Algorithm 1 requires O(N²) kernel and gradient computations but wall-clock time comparisons with baselines absent; scalability analysis missing

High hyperparameter sensitivity with substantial variation across targets (Table 2: α_X from 0.10 to 0.42; α_A from 0.20 to 0.42); unclear whether equal tuning effort invested in baseline methods; no systematic sensitivity analysis provided

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: Figure 5b shows classifier overestimation without Stein correction but root cause not deeply analyzed; formal connection between KL divergence minimization and reward estimation reliability not established; limited comparison to recent training-free baselines (DPS cited but not compared)

Theory-practice gap: theoretical analysis assumes closed-form posteriors and well-specified classifiers but robustness to classifier approximation errors not discussed; convergence properties of single-step SVGD per timestep across full diffusion trajectory not analyzed

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Low-density sampling for molecular generation is practically relevant for drug discovery
Novel computational approach: The back-and-forth correction trick elegantly avoids expensive Jacobian-vector product evaluations
Strong empirical results on molecular generation: Substantial improvements over baselines (e.g., 25.74% vs 18.67% for 5ht1b target)
Comprehensive experimental details: Appendix provides hyperparameters, visualizations, and analysis of sampling dynamics
Clear intuitive explanation: Figure 1 effectively conveys the geometric intuition of manifold-based guidance
weaknesses: Suspicious ablation study: SDG without Stein correction achieves 0.0% for jak2, suggesting unfair comparison or implementation issues rather than the gradual performance degradation expected from a method variant
Limited theoretical novelty: Proposition 3.2 is a standard variational bound (Jensen's inequality). No convergence analysis, gap bounds, or guidance on how many Stein correction steps suffice
Theory-practice disconnect: The surrogate objective Ṽ is an upper bound on V, yet the practical algorithm's connection to optimizing Ṽ is unclear and not formally proven

Single-domain validation: Despite claims of broader applications, experiments are limited to molecular generation on 3 proteins. Paper explicitly states it is 'only validated on molecular generation tasks'

Hyperparameter sensitivity not analyzed: Table 2 shows significantly different settings per protein (SNR varies 3×, α-schedules differ), suggesting per-target tuning without justification or sensitivity analysis
Missing baselines: No comparison with published training-free methods (FREEDOM, DPS), no SOC baseline, no other posterior correction approaches
Unclear cost functional formulation: Proposition 3.1 uses δ(s-t) in the cost function—the justification for this choice over direct state cost f(x,t)=α(t)log p_t(x) is not provided
Posterior approximation quality unquantified: Only one Stein update per timestep with no analysis of resulting approximation quality to true diffusion posterior
Limited novelty in components: Proposition 3.1 is standard SOC, Proposition 3.2 is standard variational inference, and Proposition 3.3 combines existing SVGD tools without new theory
RBF kernel choices unjustified: Bandwidth selection, sensitivity to kernel choice, and behavior under particle collapse are not addressed

strengths: Novel theoretical contribution showing Tweedie-based approximation is suboptimal through variational bound (Prop 3.2) with clear practical interpretation
Well-motivated connection between stochastic optimal control, Stein variational inference, and diffusion guidance with computationally efficient back-and-forth correction mechanism
Substantial empirical improvements over baselines: SDG w/o Stein correction achieves only 2.933% hit ratio while full SDG reaches 25.744% on 5ht1b, strongly validating theoretical claims
Comprehensive experimental design with multiple protein targets, diverse baselines (diffusion and non-diffusion), thorough ablation study, and mechanistic analysis of off-manifold issues
Clear and well-organized presentation with effective figures (especially Figure 1) and implementable Algorithm 1; proofs are detailed and appear technically sound
Practical training-free approach that is modular and could extend to other conditional generation settings; addresses genuine application need in low-density molecular sampling for drug discovery
weaknesses: Experimental validation limited to molecular generation only; despite claims of generality, only one application domain tested with ZINC250k dataset and three protein targets

Hyperparameter selection not well justified: α and β schedules differ substantially across targets (Table 2) without explanation of selection procedure or sensitivity analysis; unclear if this introduces tuning bias favoring SDG

Theoretical-empirical gap: Proposition 3.2 establishes upper bound on value function, but formal connection between optimizing surrogate objective and improving actual solutions is not established; bound tightness not analyzed

Off-manifold sampling issue discussed post-hoc through empirical observations (Figures 5, 9-10) rather than being formally addressed; no quantitative guarantees that Stein correction preserves manifold geometry

Improvement over MOOD baseline is modest in one case (jak2: 9.200% → 9.367%, ~1.8% relative improvement), though substantial in others; statistical significance reported but effect sizes vary considerably

Reproducibility concerns: code availability not mentioned; complex hyperparameter dependence across targets makes reproduction challenging; no runtime comparisons demonstrating computational efficiency gains claimed by the method
Missing comparisons with other posterior refinement approaches beyond Tweedie; recent training-free guidance methods [37] not compared; no ablation on the specific form of low-density cost functional
Limited analysis of failure modes, applicability constraints, or guidance for practitioners on hyperparameter selection when applying SDG to new problems

strengths: Novel theoretical framework combining Stochastic Optimal Control with Stein variational inference for training-free diffusion guidance, with formal propositions establishing value function bounds and optimal control decomposition
Creative back-and-forth Stein correction mechanism that elegantly approximates the computationally expensive SOC formulation while maintaining theoretical connection (Corollary 3.5)

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple domains (images and molecules) with systematic ablation studies (Figures 7-14) and temporal dynamics analysis demonstrating consistent improvements

Strong empirical results on important application: molecular sampling achieves novel hit ratio of 0.156 vs. near-zero for baselines (Table 2), with proven robustness under extreme low-density conditions
Honest treatment of limitations including computational overhead analysis (Table 6), reward overestimation issues, and ablation under varying low-density levels
weaknesses: Theoretical contributions lack actionable guarantees about when/why SDG outperforms alternatives; Proposition 3.2's upper bound includes loosely-bounding KL divergence term without convergence analysis
Significant computational overhead (~85% runtime increase in Table 6) not adequately justified relative to sometimes modest empirical gains (e.g., 54.0% vs 50.1% accuracy with substantial added cost)
Incremental novelty: primarily combines well-established techniques (Stein VI, SOC, score-based diffusion) through a novel cost functional rather than introducing fundamental new concepts
Limited experimental scope: images evaluated primarily on CIFAR-10, molecular sampling on only 3 protein targets; missing comparisons with recent methods like FREED and SVGD-based guidance approaches

Presentation issues: Algorithm 1 (core algorithmic contribution) relegated to appendix; relationship between theoretical Propositions and practical algorithm unclear; key assumptions (Lemma 3.3's Gaussian forward kernel) not explicitly stated in main text

Reproducibility concerns: no code availability mentioned despite method complexity; hyperparameter choices (Table 4) lack justification; cascade of approximations (Tweedie→SOC→Stein correction) has unanalyzed cumulative error

Particle update saturation (acknowledged in Section C.3.6) suggests unresolved fundamental limitations in high dimensions; guidance quality critically depends on score model accuracy without thorough dependency analysis

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: training-free guidance for low-density molecular sampling is computationally challenging and has clear applications
Rigorous mathematical framework with detailed theoretical analysis (Propositions 3.1-3.4, Lemmas 2.1-3.3, Corollary 3.5) grounded in SOC and Stein variational inference
Creative technical solution: back-and-forth Stein correction is computationally efficient compared to full SOC simulation while attempting to address posterior approximation bias
Comprehensive experiments with multiple ablation studies (Tables 2-3, Figures 5-11), testing on diverse tasks (image guidance, molecular docking), and detailed hyperparameter analysis (Table 4)
Honest treatment of computational costs and trade-offs; transparent about method complexity
Attempts to bridge theory and practice by connecting SOC theory to practical diffusion guidance
weaknesses: Weak empirical validation of core theoretical claim: Table 2 shows SDG without Stein correction achieves competitive hits ratios (0.003 on ja7 baseline comparison suggests marginal gaps), contradicting the claimed necessity of Stein correction for addressing Tweedie bias

Theory-practice gap: Theoretical analysis assumes exact score models and specific kernel forms; practical implementation violates these assumptions without analyzing error propagation or providing empirical validation that bounds predict actual performance

Proposition 3.2 provides an upper bound on value function discrepancy but does not rigorously prove the bound is tight or that correction is necessary in practice; empirical improvements are inconsistent across metrics with no clear pattern justifying added complexity
No direct experiments validating core theoretical predictions: missing experiments that directly test Proposition 3.2 or analyze when/why Stein correction is necessary versus marginal

Modest practical improvements: incremental gains (Table 1: 54.9% vs 52.2%; Table 2: often within experimental noise) do not clearly justify added hyperparameter tuning (step size α(t), guidance strength β(t)) and computational overhead (Table 6-7)

Limited and narrow application scope: molecular experiments use restrictive artificial criteria (SIM<0.4, SA<5, QED>0.5); image experiments do not specifically target low-density challenges; unclear how broadly method generalizes

Key concepts poorly defined: 'low-density regions' never formally defined; unclear whether this refers to regions with low p(x) or regions with rare samples; this ambiguity undermines clarity of central contribution

Incomplete technical justification: Stein correction step size (Eq. 28) introduces new hyperparameter without sensitivity analysis; interaction between α(t) and β(t) unexplored; justification for Polyak schedule choice absent

Missing critical ablations and baselines: no comparison to simpler regularization approaches; no comparison to other Bayesian posterior correction methods beyond Langevin; incomplete analysis of when Stein correction is truly necessary

Minimal ethical discussion: Appendix A acknowledgment of molecular generation dual-use concerns is superficial; lacks discussion of safeguards, access controls, or detection methods appropriate for drug discovery application
Unquantified approximation errors: Lemma 3.3 assumes accurate score models but typical score model errors are not analyzed; error propagation through approximation cascade is not studied

Presentation issues: paper attempts too much (images and molecules) without depth in either application; notation inconsistencies (⊕ operator undefined until later); weak justification for low-density cost formulation (Eq. 3) jump from SOC (Eq. 2)

strengths: Strong theoretical foundation rigorously connecting stochastic optimal control with Stein variational inference to develop training-free diffusion guidance with formal justification (Propositions 3.1-3.4)

Novel back-and-forth Stein correction mechanism that addresses the suboptimality of Tweedie-based approximations while remaining computationally practical by avoiding expensive Jacobian-vector products

Comprehensive experimental validation across two distinct domains (images and molecules) with multiple evaluation metrics, ablation studies, and analysis of robustness across varying low-density levels

Consistent empirical improvements over training-free baselines, with particularly strong results on molecular low-density sampling tasks where standard methods fail (Table 2: 0.239 vs 0.956 hit ratio)
Clear presentation of motivation and technical content with well-designed visualizations (Figures 1-2) and detailed algorithmic description (Algorithm 1)
Appropriate treatment of broader impact and research ethics regarding potential drug discovery applications
Thorough experimental setup details in appendices enabling reproducibility (hyperparameters in Table 4, computational analysis in Tables 6-7)
weaknesses: Theoretical guarantees depend on quality of score models, but practical degradation when score models are poor is not thoroughly investigated; convergence behavior of Monte Carlo approximations in Lemma 3.3 not characterized

Improvements in most standard benchmarks are incremental (2-5% on image tasks in Table 1), though more substantial on specialized molecular low-density tasks; magnitude of practical significance unclear
Evaluation limited to image and molecular domains; generalization to video, 3D shapes, text, and other modalities unexplored, limiting scope claims
Computational overhead non-negligible (~2x slowdown in Table 6); comparison limited to other training-free methods with little discussion of relative cost versus trained guidance approaches

Hyperparameter sensitivity analysis is limited despite introducing multiple new hyperparameters (α scheduling, β guidance strength, ε step size, N particles); generalization across domains not demonstrated
Novel graph-based diffusion prior (Equation 27) for molecular generation appears somewhat ad-hoc with limited theoretical justification beyond empirical motivation
Reward model training details sparse and distribution shift from clean training data to low-density sampling regions not explicitly addressed, despite this being the core motivation
